meaningMnemonic: A turtle that stands up isn't a turtle anymore. It's evolved into a monster. What kind of monster? A dragon ! Rawwwr.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means wind .
The radical blade and the kanji blade are exactly the same. Hints Please, just know your radicals. Please!
readingMnemonic: When you stab your blade into an enemy you shout " Hah ( は )!" You've gotta get some oomph behind that thrust, after all. Hints Hah! Slash! Hah! Thrust! Hah! Parry! There you go — now you're really using that blade!

meaningMnemonic: You put a stone into a wrap of some kind. This wrap happens to be a cannon , and you're shooting off the stone, just like I used to do to boats with the cannon we had growing up for some reason. Hints This makes a lot of sense when you think about it, right? The muzzle of the cannon wraps around the rock, then you shoot the rock. Boom!
readingMnemonic: You aim the cannon at your own ho me ( ほう ). You don't want to have a home anymore, you want to become a pirate, live on a boat, and (of course) shoot cannons all day long. Hints Watch as the cannon goes off, the rock hurtles into your home. And just like that, there is a huge, rock-shaped hole in it. You'll have to shoot a few more rocks at your home with this cannon before it's completely gone.

meaningMnemonic: A bamboo thing you put on your head to stand taller would probably be a hat. A bamboo hat is probably one of those hats you think of when you think of rice farmers, a conical hat . Hints You know the ones I'm talking about? They're cone-shaped, sort of, and they go on your head, keeping the sun off your face.
readingMnemonic: A conical hat is kind of like an umbrella on your head. What's the reading for "umbrella" in Japanese? Why, it's kasa ( かさ )! Hints Think about a bamboo umbrella on your head. They're pretty similar in shape, after all.

meaningMnemonic: The dragon radical is the same as this kanji, which is dragon . Hints Not to dragon with it, but make sure you know your radicals so you know your kanji!
readingMnemonic: Imagine a dragon . You are talking to it, which is already pretty strange, but as you're talking, he turns into the Street Fighter character Ryu ( りゅう ). Hints Then imagine after his transformation he attacks you using his Street Fighter moves. "Hadouken!"

meaningMnemonic: Your fingers told you that a flood last evening would draw close . There was nothing you could do to stop it, it seemed to be be imminent , coming in the darkness of the evening. Hints Think back to last evening, when your fingers twitched and twisted, warning you as the flood started to draw close.
readingMnemonic: Luckily whenever you sense a flood starting to draw close , Satsu ki ( さつ ) prepares a raft. Remember Satsuki? Such a talented little girl. I guess floods are common enough that she's learned to make rafts? Hints This one is barely big enough for two people, so you have to draw close if you want to fit. Kind of uncomfortable, but it's better than being caught in an imminent flood.

meaningMnemonic: A thread is all that's keeping Wolverine and a pig from falling off the edge of a cliff. Wolverine and this pig had no relation prior to this, but after such a harrowing experience they're sure to form a deep bond. Hints Picture Wolverine and a pig hanging precariously over the edge of this cliff. What a crazy way to form a relation! It'll all be for naught if the thread snaps, though…
readingMnemonic: Just as it seems like they'll be able to climb back from the edge , the thread snaps, and Wolverine and his new pig friend plunge to a tragic en d ( えん ). What a shame — they had just begun to form such a friendly relation , too… Hints Moral of the story: stay away from edges, because they might spell the end for you and all your earthly relations.

meaningMnemonic: If someone puts a blade to your heart , you're going to have a rough time. They leave it there, for a long time. They aren't going to cut you, but you can't move. You have to endure the pain and conceal your discomfort with the situation. Hints To endure something is to conceal how it makes you feel, after all. Now imagine there's a blade pressed close to your heart. Try to endure the pain and conceal your emotions, or your heart might be cut.
readingMnemonic: Learning to endure and conceal is all part of your nin ja ( にん ) training. You must learn to stay totally still, without breathing — you have to be able to endure this if you want to conceal yourself. Hints No one knows better than a ninja how enduring and concealing are closely related. Go ahead, hold your breath and try walking soundlessly around your house, concealing your footsteps. Not easy to endure, is it?

meaningMnemonic: A gold pool is where you're going to go fishing . Because, if the pool is gold, hopefully the fish are too. Hints Imagine yourself fishing in a gold pool, catching golden fish. What a great fishing spot this is.
readingMnemonic: You caught a couple of gold fish. Two ( つ ) gold fish, actually! Hints Count your golden fish. They're so nice! They're also worth their weight in gold, because, well, they are gold.

meaningMnemonic: The animal that hangs out in melon patches is the elusive fox ! They like to steal melons then come back into town disguised as human melon sellers. Foxes are tricky like that. Hints Imagine seeing a red fox scampering through a melon patch trying to take melons with it.
readingMnemonic: If you want to stop fox es from stealing your melons you can get one of those kits that neigh ( きつね ) when one is around. The kits neigh when they sense a fox, but because it sounds like a horse the fox won't run. But you'll be able to get out there and take your melons back! Hints Imagine buying kits that neigh and putting them around your melon patch to warn you when foxes are around.

meaningMnemonic: The good luck radical and the good luck kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: For good luck , you keep special kits ( きつ ) in your kitch en ( きち ). These kitchen kits contain good luck charms. Hints Your good luck kitchen kits have charms that say things like, "good food," "good company," and "good luck not cutting off your fingers with kitchen knives."

meaningMnemonic: You hop on your scooter while wearing horns and zoom off toward a barracks on the moon — a journey which requires you to go upstream on a raging lunar river. Are you up to the challenge? Hints Actually, yes. The lunar military's given you a tricked-out aquatic space scooter that can go upstream even through the toughest rapids. The horns are just part of your uniform — all soldiers on the moon wear them.
readingMnemonic: As you go upstream on your scooter, you notice that this lunar river is full of so ap ( そ )! You're basically riding your scooter upstream in a giant, frothing, soapy bubble bath. Are all rivers on the moon like this? Hints Feel your eyes begin to sting as the soapy water splashes into them. Going upstream to the moon barracks is shaping up to be quite an ordeal, but look on the bright side: all this soap is going to get you and your scooter really clean!

meaningMnemonic: The part of rice that stand s up tall in the air (at the end of the stalks) is the grains . Hints If you think about this one it'll make good sense. Just imagine rice stalks standing up into the air.
readingMnemonic: You have a box of grains . Ryuu ( りゅう ) from Street Fighter is doing training by punching the grains to strengthen his fingers. Hints He has his hands flat, and stabs his hands into the grains. Yah! Yah! Yah!

meaningMnemonic: Your long hair is your friend . It's your hair and you're so proud of it. Hints Just feel your hair, it's such a good friend, and you wish it was longer.
readingMnemonic: Who gave you this hair? Probably the great 神 ( かみ ) of hair. You deserve this great hair. Hints Pretend to pray to the great hair 神 . What is his reply? Does he give you more hair?

meaningMnemonic: An axe is stuck into the ground on a hill . Hints Imagine climbing up the hill. The sun is coming up behind the axe,  silhouetting the whole thing very nicely.
readingMnemonic: You reach the top of the hill and realize the entire hill is covered in cu cumbers ( きゅう ). The axe has a little note on it that says "Cucumber Hill Axe - Please Use." Hints You take the axe out of the hill and cut off some cucumber to eat. Mm mm!

meaningMnemonic: The ladle radical and the ladle kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: You use a ladle to distribute soup. But as you're ladling you find something odd floating in the soup. It's... a toe ( と )! You scream, dropping the ladle and the toe on the ground. Hints Your mom comes rushing in and smacks you on the head. "Fool!" she says, "This is toe soup, what did you think you'd ladle up?!" Oops.

meaningMnemonic: Looking at the moon , you notice it's grown a bunch of branch es. Wait, are those all… limbs ?! Hints You feel absolutely terrified looking at the moon with all its branches consisting of limbs, lifelessly flopping around. How did this happen?
readingMnemonic: After some consideration, you know who put all those limb s on the moon. It must've been none other than the moon shee p ( し )! Hints The moon sheep are always up to no good, so this must all have been devised by them. Those darn moon sheep!

meaningMnemonic: The measurement radical and the measurement kanji are exactly the same. Hints If you make sure to know the radicals, you'll also make sure to know the kanji too, automagically.
readingMnemonic: "Calculate your enemy's position with accurate measurement ," is more or less what Sun ( すん ) Tzu said, I think. The guy wrote The Art of War, you know. When Sun says measurements are important, you don't question him. Hints Imagine Mr. Sun measuring distances and rations and whatnot just before going to war — maps, compasses, all kinds of measurement devices piled on his war table. Also, don't forget that in Chinese Sun is pronounced more like "soon."

meaningMnemonic: No one can say what a scooter weighs in grains of rice — it's a mystery ! Hints Imagine lifting a scooter, hefting it, trying to guess its weight in grains of rice. At least 100 grains, I'd say. But no one can say, really. It's a total mystery.
readingMnemonic: To get to the bottom of this mystery , you use a nozzle ( なぞ ). You pass rice through the nozzle one grain at a time, so you can figure out precisely how many grains of rice are equal to the weight of a scooter. Hints Imagine watching this little nozzle squeeze out the rice, grain by grain, onto a scale. And imagine the boredom you'd feel watching that… But yes, you really can resolve any rice-based measurement mysteries thanks to this nozzle.

meaningMnemonic: You see a thread -covered hill , but it's all lumpy and weird. You approach it to take a closer look, and you see it's actually a huge net with a bunch of stuff caught in it: fish, cats, tree branches. All this random stuff is what's making the net look so lumpy! Hints You'll need to differentiate this from 綱 , which uses the same radicals (though 綱 has a real hill radical). Just remember that the "hill" in this one is all weird and lumpy because it's a net with a bunch of stuff caught in it.
readingMnemonic: This net is creating a serious obstacle to you mow ing ( もう ) the grass, which is what you originally came here to do. For now, you're just going to have to mow around the net, since it has way too much stuff in it for you to be able to drag it away. Hints Imagine the awkwardness of trying to mow the grass around this big, lumpy, writhing net full of loudly meowing cats, flopping fish, and goodness knows what else.

meaningMnemonic: The tree has an omen growing from it, one single peach that is the size of a house. Inside is a child who will save the village from demons. Hints Of course, this tree omen of a peach refers to momotaro, the little boy who was born from a peach (you should look it up if you don't know this children's story).
readingMnemonic: If momo taro ( もも ) wasn't enough, think about the peach growing larger and larger. You want it to grow bigger, so you yell at it: " MO RE! MO RE!" ( もも ). Hints It grows bigger everytime you say "MORE MORE" twice. If you say it just once, it stays the same.

meaningMnemonic: The grain you cut off a tree with a knife is a pear . You've found some particularly big, sturdy ones, which is why you need the help of your knife. These pears are sure to be super juicy and delicious, but you need some extra tools to get them off the tree. Hints Imagine looking up at a tree full of thick-stemmed, jumbo-size pears. You pull out your knife and get ready to hack them all down, one by one.
readingMnemonic: As you cut the pear s down, you can't help but gnash ( なし ) your teeth. You want to eat these pears right now. You gnash and grind and wait though, because you want to have them all down before you start the feast. Hints Imagine a beautiful, ripe pear in your mind. Now gnash your teeth. Mmm. You want to eat a pear right now, don't you?

meaningMnemonic: The woman servant is the lower ranking princess . The queen is no servant. Hecks no. Just the princess, because she's a servant to what her parents tell her to do. Hints Just imagine a princess saying "UGH, I'm just like a servant, I have to do all the crap you tell me." Then, all the servants roll their eyes, because, really, she's a princess, lucky duck.
readingMnemonic: The princess goes on to do whatever she wants. She tells the real servants, "Don't tell my daddy, the king, I did this. He may ( ひめ ) not like it." Hints The servants all know they should tell the king, because the princess is a servant to the king, just as they are, plus they don't want to lose their heads.

meaningMnemonic: You use your fingers when you're in private to use an arrow to push open things. Hints You're in private in your own room, no one else is around. Now you wrap your fingers around this big arrow, and you push open your door, your curtains, your windows. It's weird, but you really enjoy this.
readingMnemonic: Your favorite thing to push open is your own eye ( あい ). You take the arrow into your fingers and gently push each lid open until you can see. Hints Picture the arrow in your hands. You're facing a mirror, but you can't see because you're about to push open your eyes. The anticipation is killing you, push them open now!

meaningMnemonic: A woman loves her catapult for some good ol' fashioned recreation . Hints You ask the woman what she does for fun... for recreation. She says, she goes out and shoots her catapult.
readingMnemonic: Her favorite thing to shoot at with her catapult for recreation is Go dzilla ( ご ). Hints Get out of here, Godzilla! I'm gonna shoot you.

meaningMnemonic: The leader of the temple isn't a monk like you'd expect. It's a samurai , who protects the monks in return for prayers that keep him safe. Hints You walk up to a temple and you're surprised to find that there's a samurai guarding it. Talk to him for a while so he can tell you why he has been doing this job. He's quite a nice guy, actually.
readingMnemonic: The reading is samurai , which should be easy enough to remember. Hints If you know the meaning you know the reading as well! That doesn't happen too often with kanji, so consider yourself lucky!

meaningMnemonic: From my mouth I have told you seven times not to do that. Now I have to scold you. Hints SEVEN TIMES! You'd think you'd learn.
readingMnemonic: What were you doing wrong that caused me to scold you? You were feeding the 鹿 ( しか ). If you feed them they'll never be able to feed themselves! Hints Imagine yourself feeding the deer, then getting scolded (or you doing the scolding to someone else feeding the deer, whichever works best).

meaningMnemonic: You have mouth vines , so you shout ! It's hard for you to talk normally, and even harder for people to understand you unless you shout. Hints You were born with mouth vines (a rare condition where your mouth is always full of vines), so you've been shouting all your life. And yet people still can't hear you. It's very frustrating.
readingMnemonic: You need to shout so that people can understand you through the mouth vines. You shout, " きょう と !" because you hear there is a temple there for people with your condition. Hints Imagine the word きょうと not coming out clearly because of your mouth vines. People can only hear the きょう part, so they don't know where you want to go. SHOUT LOUDER! きょうと！

meaningMnemonic: A flowers fang is the bud that comes out of the ground. It's like a little fang, coming from the earth, and it will become a flower someday. This is a little sprout . Hints Imagine a bunch of these. They look like big fangs poking out of the ground (that is, until they bloom and get into the air).
readingMnemonic: When the sprout gets out of the ground and opens up, instead of a flower there is a human-looking 目 ( め ), looking right at you. Hints You look at all the sprouts. They have all turned into 目 s, looking straight at you. You're terrified.

meaningMnemonic: The mountain wind coming down from the mountains is very fierce. It is so fierce it's a lot like a storm . Well, it is a storm, really. Hints If you think about it makes sense. Those mountain winds that come down from the mountain are cold and windy and nasty. When they mix with warmer air down below, it creates a nasty storm .
readingMnemonic: A storm is nothing to scoff at. If you get hit by the storm and get all wet and nasty and electrocuted, you're bound to get a rash ( あらし ). Hints The rash comes from being wet and not drying off when you get home. Your skin gets irritated by this moisture.

meaningMnemonic: Rain on a rice paddy means only one thing... thunder ! Get off the rice paddy! There's nothing but you to attract the thunder! Hints Imagine hearing the thunder closing in on you as you frantically try to escape the rice paddy. RUN!!!
readingMnemonic: You can’t run fast enough to escape the thunder , so you decide to hide under a pile of… rye ( らい )?! Hints This rye will save your life. It’s just you and this pile of rye now. Take a deeeeep breath in, and really smell the thunder and rye in the air. You’re fine. You’re cozy. This rye will be your savior.

meaningMnemonic: When dirt and flowers suit one another, the flowers grow so tall that they make a tower ! A flower tower made of flower power! Hints Imagine walking in the woods and coming across a huge tower made of flowers. It goes so high you can hardly see the top.
readingMnemonic: The only place flowers grow into tower s like this is in とう きょう . とうきょう dirt is the best. とうきょう flowers are the best. Thus, you end up with a lot of とうきょう towers. Hints How do you think the とうきょう tower came to be, anyway? It was once a big flower tower. They just replaced it with metal later. BOOM! History bomb, you're welcome.

meaningMnemonic: The slide to get off this jet is a beautiful, brilliant vermilion color. Hints Vermilion is like an orange red, which is perfect for visibility purposes.
readingMnemonic: You jump onto the vermilion slide. It's actually more of a steep chu te ( しゅ ). And... oh... urp... it's making you sick. Hints The vermilion chute spits you out and you spit out your lunch. And it looks vermilion. Uh oh. Hospital. Please.

meaningMnemonic: A feather is on a rice paddy , and they are attached together . You put a feather on a rice paddy to create a giant airplane. Flawed, sure. But, this rice paddy + feather is going to be one wing of your amazing aircraft. Hints Imagine a wing that is made of a rice paddy and a feather put together. Doesn't make sense, looks ugly, and probably will not fly. Imagine it anyways. It is your wing.
readingMnemonic: To make the feather and rice paddy stick together you need some kind of sticking agent. This time we find the original bird that the feather came from and grab its eggs. We break the eggs open and use the yolk ( よく ). It's pretty sticky, but still probably not aircraft safe. Hints Imagine using the yolks to stick everything together. It's all over your hands, and things are pretty nasty.

meaningMnemonic: A challenge ( 挑戦 ) someone is someone who is going to challenge you. They are a challenger .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 腕相撲の挑戦者は、握力を見せつけるために、右手で林檎を潰してみせました。
sentences.english: The arm‐wrestling challenger crushed an apple in his right hand, showing off the strength of his right hand.

meaningMnemonic: Line up house counters and you'll see that all the houses you've counted are the same across the board . It also turns them into a row of houses .
readingMnemonic: This is a combination of the words 軒 and 並 that you've already learned, so you should be able to read this word too. Just note that for 並 , the み in なみ is sticking out! While you might sometimes see this written 軒並 , 軒並み is way more common.

sentences.japanese: IT関連の株価が軒並み下落しました。
sentences.english: IT-related stock prices fell across the board.

meaningMnemonic: One wing is just a part of the bird or plane it's attached to. But that one wing plays a role that's very important! This word usually comes up in the phrase 〜の一翼を担う (to play a part in…).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 大きなプロジェクトの一翼を担えることになりました。
sentences.english: I have been entrusted to take on part of the large project.

meaningMnemonic: When you help with your power , you are providing assistance and support . Note that this is a formal word that’s mostly used in professional situations. It implies that someone has done something substantial for you.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: You really need some assistance with this lock ( りょく ). You are certain that world peace and eternal happiness lie behind this one lock. But no one is willing to support you in opening it. What a cruel world.

sentences.japanese: 助力をあおぐ
sentences.english: to ask for help

sentences.japanese: 助力をいただく
sentences.english: to receive assistance

sentences.japanese: 助力を求める
sentences.english: to ask for assistance

sentences.japanese: 助力を得る
sentences.english: to receive assistance

sentences.japanese: 専門家の助力
sentences.english: assistance of an expert

sentences.japanese: 詳しい人の助力
sentences.english: assistance of someone knowledgeable

sentences.japanese: 他の人の助力
sentences.english: assistance of other people

sentences.japanese: 助力に感謝する
sentences.english: to express gratitude for assistance

sentences.japanese: 父の助力のおかげです。
sentences.english: That's thanks to help of my father.

sentences.japanese: 他人の助力が有ったから出来たことです。
sentences.english: This was only possible with the help of others.

sentences.japanese: 友人の助力で、四年間で大学を出ることが出来そうです。
sentences.english: With the help of a friend, it seems like I can get out of college after four years.

meaningMnemonic: A sleep bed is where you sleep. Where do you sleep? In a bed , probably. This can refer to any kind of sleeping place , including a bed, futon, or even an animal's nest or den. You'll often see it in literature, in phrases like 寝床に入る (to get into bed). When you're talking about your bed in casual conversation, you'll probably just say ベッド .
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn the second kun'yomi reading for 床 . You take とこ and rendaku it into どこ . How do you remember this? Just think about your bed. Then wonder, " where ( どこ ) is it?"

sentences.japanese: 寝床に入ったとたん、宿題があることを思い出した。
sentences.english: The moment I got into bed, I remembered I had homework.

sentences.japanese: 寝床の中で大人しくしているほど、僕は聞き分けのいい子ではなかった。
sentences.english: I wasn't the kind of obedient child who would quietly stay in bed.

sentences.japanese: 猫は寝床の上で小さく身を丸め、静かな寝息を立てていた。
sentences.english: The cat lay curled up on its bed, breathing softly in its sleep.

sentences.japanese: 夜更けの雨はやむ気配もなく、私は寝床の中でその単調な響きに耳を傾けていた。
sentences.english: The late-night rain showed no sign of stopping, and I lay in bed listening to its monotonous sound.

meaningMnemonic: Go upstream through the currents of time to reach something in the past — this is called being retroactive . 遡及 is a formal, technical word used when something is applied retroactively. You'll mostly see it in legal or administrative contexts when discussing rules or effects that are being applied to past actions or situations.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You know these readings — no need to retroactively learn any new readings for old kanji here.

sentences.japanese: 遡及適用
sentences.english: retroactive application

sentences.japanese: 遡及請求
sentences.english: retroactive claim

sentences.japanese: 遡及的
sentences.english: retroactive

sentences.japanese: 年金の遡及請求について説明を受けました。
sentences.english: I received an explanation about retroactive pension claims.

sentences.japanese: この法律は過年度へ遡及適用されることはありません。
sentences.english: This law will not be applied retroactively to past fiscal years.

sentences.japanese: 給与規定の改定は、非遡及的なものになる予定です。
sentences.english: The revision of the salary regulations is expected to be non-retroactive.

sentences.japanese: 当時は気づかなかった小さな言葉や視線が、今になって意味を持ち、静かだった彼の心を遡及的な怒りが焼きつくしていった。
sentences.english: Small words and glances he hadn't noticed at the time now took on meaning, and a retroactive anger burned away his once-quiet heart.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. But it also has a secondary reading you haven't learned, so here’s a mnemonic for it: Blade in hand, you charge at your foes hollering " Yah ! Eee ! Baa !" ( やいば ). As the blade cuts through them, you cry "Yah! Eee! Baa!" even louder. This battle cry always fuels your fury and doubles the force of your swinging blade. "Yah! Eee! Baa!" While both readings relate to blades, they have slightly different uses. は is used for any cutting tool's blade or edge, whereas やいば is a little old-fashioned and specifically refers to the blades of swords or knives, often in literary contexts.

sentences.japanese: 心配は要りませんよ、患者さん。私のこの手術用メスの鋭い刃で、すぐに盲腸を取ってあげますからね。
sentences.english: Don't worry, my patient. I can immediately remove your appendix with the sharp blade of my surgical scalpel.

meaningMnemonic: Gold hair is blond hair . Makes sense!
readingMnemonic: This word uses 髪 's on'yomi reading はつ , but it changes to ぱつ due to the ん sound before it. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it: Admiring your beautiful blond hair , someone comes along and pats ( ぱつ ) it. Actually, this is pretty normal for you — some random stranger pats your hair almost every day. It's just the price you pay for those gorgeous golden locks.

sentences.japanese: 金髪になりたかったので、コカコーラで髪を脱色しました。
sentences.english: I wanted to be blonde so I bleached my hair with Coca-Cola.

meaningMnemonic: Both wing s are both wings ! There are two and you have them all!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 二遊間、外野の両翼のポジションはまだ空いています。
sentences.english: A ball was hit between the second baseman and the shortstop, and both outfield positions are still vacant.

meaningMnemonic: A can coffee ( コーヒー ) is coffee that's in a can. That's canned coffee or can coffee .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 彼らは、とても美味い缶コーヒーを販売して、大儲けしている。
sentences.english: They’re making a killing selling delicious canned coffee.

meaningMnemonic: A big cannon is... wait for it... just a cannon . I guess all cannons are big, right? At least when you compare them to guns.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 大砲がズドーンと鳴り響き、男は三人の子どもたちを残したまま逝ってしまいました。

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means sink so the verb vocab version is to sink something or to submerge something . This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. So instead of describing something sinking on its own, you use 沈める when you sink an enemy ship or submerge yourself in a bathtub. You know this because you can't sink anything until you get that mail ( める ) saying, "Yes, proceed with sinking!" You've got to have that mail if you want to sink something, or else everyone will blame you for the missing ship — or for you disappearing under the water.
readingMnemonic: When you sink something, like a battleship, you go on and say: " she's ( しず ) sunk, I sunk her." That's like your tagline, or something. You say it for some reason because you think it's cool.

Well, if something has a nothing relation , it's probably unrelated . 無縁 describes having no ties with something else — you're utterly divorced from or uninvolved with that thing. For example, maybe you grew up in 宗教とは無縁な家庭 (a totally nonreligious household), or maybe you live お酒とは無縁な生活 (a life free of alcohol). Whatever the case, this thing is totally alien to you.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. 朱 refers to vermilion , a bright red color with a slight orange tint, and can also be translated as scarlet red . It's common in Japanese culture — you'll often see it on shrine gates and lacquerware, for example.
readingMnemonic: The reading can be either the on'yomi or kun'yomi reading, so you have a choice there. Since you learned the on'yomi しゅ with the kanji already, let's learn the あけ reading now. あけ sounds like the beginning of 開ける (to open). So imagine you 開け る ( あけ ) a person up, to see what color they are inside. Turns out it's vermilion ! Uh… you shouldn't open people up like that. 朱 is mostly read しゅ , but it can also be read あけ in certain phrases, like 朱に染まる , which means "to be covered in blood" (literally, "to be dyed in vermilion").
